chemicals.concentration_notes: Soluble oxalates are present in varying degrees throughout all parts of the rhubarb plant2. However, the toxins are most highly concentrated in the leaves14. While the stalks (stems) contain a significantly lower concentration of oxalates—which is why humans can safely eat them—they are still considered risky for cats.
chemicals.description: Unlike insoluble oxalates (which primarily cause localized mouth pain), soluble oxalates are absorbed directly from the gastrointestinal tract into the cat's bloodstream12. Once in the blood, these oxalate salts bind aggressively with the body's systemic calcium, resulting in a sudden and dangerous drop in blood calcium levels (hypocalcemia).
chemicals.name: Soluble oxalates (specifically, oxalic acid and soluble oxalate salts)

description:
Rhubarb (Rheum rhabarbarum) is dangerous for cats. While people often eat the stalks in pies or jams, the entire plant is toxic to cats. The leaves are the most poisonous part because they contain the highest level of harmful compounds called soluble oxalates.

When a cat eats rhubarb, these oxalates are absorbed into the blood and quickly grab onto the body’s calcium. This causes a sudden drop in blood calcium, which can lead to tremors or seizures. These compounds also form tiny crystals that can get stuck in the kidneys and cause serious damage.

Symptoms often start with drooling, vomiting, or diarrhea. As the poisoning gets worse, a cat might become very weak, lose coordination, or show signs of kidney trouble like drinking more water than usual. If you suspect your cat ate any part of a rhubarb plant, please contact a veterinarian immediately.
name: Rhubarb
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: oxalic acid and soluble oxalate salts; leaves contain the highest concentration; stalks contain moderate amounts
Mechanism: soluble oxalates bind calcium in the bloodstream, causing hypocalcaemia; calcium oxalate crystals precipitate in kidney tubules causing renal damage
Symptoms: drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, muscle tremors (from hypocalcaemia); kidney damage may cause increased thirst and urination
Leaves are the most dangerous part; even small amounts can cause serious symptoms in cats
Contact your vet if your cat ingests any part of the rhubarb plant

symptoms.name: Drooling, inappetence (loss of appetite), vomiting, and diarrhea
symptoms.notes: Small ingestions, such as a mere taste or nibble of the plant, often result only in mild gastrointestinal upset1. However, with larger ingestions, these initial GI symptoms act as a precursor to much more serious systemic poisoning.
symptoms.onset: Initial signs typically appear shortly after ingestion

symptoms.name: Lethargy, extreme weakness, ataxia (loss of coordination), tremors, and seizures
symptoms.notes: These severe neurological signs occur because the soluble oxalates in rhubarb absorb into the blood and aggressively bind to the cat's systemic calcium.
symptoms.onset: Develops progressively as the toxins are absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the bloodstre

symptoms.name: Bloody urine, changes in thirst and urination (polyuria/polydipsia), oliguria (abnormally low urine production), anuria
symptoms.notes: As the soluble oxalates bind with the body's calcium, the resulting calcium oxalate crystals can precipitate and become lodged within the renal tubules1. This physically damages the kidneys and can rarely lead to life-threatening acute renal failure.
symptoms.onset: Delayed; develops secondary to the absorption of the toxin and subsequent crystal formation

treatments.description: The veterinarian will medically induce vomiting to empty the stomach of the plant material. This is followed by administering a dose of activated charcoal along with a cathartic to bind to any remaining toxins in the gastrointestinal tract and speed up their elimination.
treatments.name: Emesis Induction and Activated Charcoal
treatments.notes: This decontamination step is recommended for exposures consisting of more than just a small taste or nibble.

treatments.description: The cat is hospitalized and administered continuous IV fluids for 24 to 48 hours.
treatments.name: Intravenous (IV) Fluid Therapy
treatments.notes: This is a critical step to flush the toxins from the system and protect the kidneys from damage, as the calcium oxalate crystals can precipitate and lodge within the renal tubules, leading to acute renal failure.

treatments.description: The veterinary team will administer calcium gluconate directly into the cat's bloodstream.
treatments.name: Intravenous Calcium Gluconate
treatments.notes: This specific treatment is indicated to directly counteract hypocalcemia (dangerously low blood calcium levels) caused by the soluble oxalates binding with the body's natural calcium.

treatments.description: While the cat is hospitalized, the veterinary team will conduct ongoing bloodwork and tests to monitor the cat's renal (kidney) indices.
treatments.name: Hospitalization and Renal Indices Monitoring
treatments.notes: Close monitoring is necessary to evaluate if the cat is developing clinical signs of acute kidney damage, such as bloody urine, changes in thirst, or lack of urine production (oliguria/anuria)
